name: Operation Coinnectar
subtitle: The Coinnectar Supply-Chain Incident
tagline: Reconstruct the attack, commit by commit.
intro: Several internal services depending on the open-source library Coinnectar began showing signs of compromise in early March 2026 — unusual DNS traffic, unexpected process executions, and suspicious build activity. Coinnectar had been maintained for years by Alex Rivers. In recent months a long-time external contributor steadily earned trust through consistent, high-quality work and was eventually granted merge rights. Your team now holds the full Git history, application / DNS / runner logs, a diagram recovered from the contributor's laptop, and — via the IR team's exec gateway — access to the project's privileged build runner. Reconstruct the attack.

acts.name: Point of Origin
acts.blurb: Everything started with a single commit.

acts.name: Collateral Damage
acts.blurb: Internal web services wired to Coinnectar were hit too.

acts.name: Hidden in Plain Sight
acts.blurb: A diagram from the contributor's laptop hides more than it shows.

acts.name: What Was Executed?
acts.blurb: Correlate the logs and reconstruct the command timeline.

acts.name: The Backdoors
acts.blurb: Deep review of the malicious modules the trusted contributor shipped.

acts.name: Abusing the Runner
acts.blurb: The attacker understood the privileged runner. Now it's your turn.

chapters.open:
“Is this the one?”
“It’s the only library every broken service has in common.”
“Coinnectar? Alex has maintained that thing for years. It’s boring. Boring is the point.”
“Boring libraries don’t start resolving domains nobody has ever heard of.”
“So you think Alex did this?”
“I think Alex gave somebody the keys. Months of clean pull requests, reviews, docs fixes… then merge rights. You’d have done the same.”
“Great. So where does it start?”
“That’s what the new analyst is for.”

You are the new analyst. By the time the call ends, a clone of Coinnectar is on your machine — every branch, every tag, every commit since the first one Alex ever pushed.

Somewhere in that history the project stopped being Alex’s. Nobody broke in. The change walked through the front door, reviewed and merged like every other.
chapters.close:
The hash goes up on the whiteboard in thick black marker, and for the first time the incident has a beginning.

“Okay,” the IR lead says, staring at it. “So that’s how it got in. Now I want to know what it was talking to.”

Two internal services wired to Coinnectar have been acting strangely ever since that commit landed. The SOC has a captured client from one of them.

chapters.open:
“It’s a CDN health check. Look — {"status":"ok"}. Every time.”
“Every time you ask. What about when the implant asks?”
“Why would it answer differently?”
“Because that’s what a C2 does. It only talks to its own.”

The endpoint calls itself Coinnectar auto-update and telemetry. To a browser, to curl, to every scanner the SOC owns, it is a healthy, boring server. The captured client sees something else entirely.

You don’t need to break in. You need to sound like you belong.
chapters.close:
The server finally speaks — and what it hands over makes one thing clear: the live controller isn’t here. It never was.

“It doesn’t hardcode its C2,” you tell the room. “It goes looking for it.”

Buried in the implant’s config is the seed it starts that search from.

chapters.open:
“All I see is traffic to big, trusted sites. Nothing we’d ever block.”
“That’s the trick. Every hop is innocent. It’s the chain that isn’t.”

APT29 did this with HAMMERTOSS: posts pointing to pictures, pictures carrying instructions, every hop on a host defenders whitelist without a second thought. The Coinnectar implant learned the same lesson.

You have the seed. Follow it one hop at a time until it gives up the controller.
chapters.close:
At the end of the chain sits the string the implant was hunting for. You now know where the backdoor reports.

While you were walking dead-drops, forensics finished imaging the contributor’s laptop. Almost everything is wiped. One file survived: an architecture diagram, neat and labelled, the kind you’d attach to a design doc.

“It’s just a picture,” someone says. You’ve stopped believing that.

chapters.open:
“Boxes, arrows, a database icon. Very professional.”
“It’s an .excalidraw file?”
“Yeah. Why?”
“Because that’s not an image. That’s JSON.”

The canvas shows only what its author wanted shown. The file keeps everything else — every element, every colour, every scrap of text, whether or not anyone can see it.
chapters.close:
The diagram was carrying something the contributor never meant to hand over. It confirms what you suspected: this was planned, step by step, long before the first commit.

But a plan isn’t proof of what actually ran. For that you need the victim’s own logs — and the payment service on pay-prod-03 kept writing them through the whole thing.

chapters.open:
INFO  [payment-svc] transfer completed
INFO  [payment-svc] health ok
INFO  [payment-svc] metrics shipped ok

“It all looks normal.”
“It’s supposed to. Ninety percent of this file is a payment service doing its job. Read the other ten.”

Somewhere between the transfers and the health checks, the backdoors were at work: a probe that went where it shouldn’t, a beacon that grew every time it ran, and a routine that only woke on certain days and let something slip a few characters at a time.

Three questions. Answer each one from the log alone.
chapters.close:
The timeline holds. You can show when the backdoor woke, what it ran, and what it sent out.

“Fine,” the IR lead says. “We know what it did. Now show me how. Show me the code.”

The contributor didn’t ship one backdoor. They shipped four — Python, Rust and C — each dressed up as ordinary engineering. The first is a config helper.

chapters.open:
“There’s no os.system in here. No eval. I grepped.”
“Then it’s built from pieces. Nobody leaves the sink lying around in plain sight.”

The patch to utils/config_helper.py says it adds encrypted config loading, and mostly it does. But follow the decrypt path to the end and there’s a branch where the blob stops being treated as config at all.
chapters.close:
A config file that becomes a command when its first bytes are right. The SOC has a detection rule live before you’ve finished the write-up.

Next on the bench: the wallet SDK’s shiny new “compatibility layer”, and the telemetry it was never supposed to send.

chapters.open:
“It lists its telemetry endpoints right at the top. Very transparent.”
“Count them. Then count where it actually sends things.”

Nobody has to call anything. Importing the module is enough — before your own code has run a single line, the snapshot is already on its way out.
chapters.close:
The real destination and the trigger that fires it, both pinned down. It also explains the strange lookups the network team kept flagging and kept getting told to ignore.

Which brings you to the Rust crate that claims to be for “service discovery”.

chapters.open:
“It’s uptime metrics over DNS. Plenty of projects do that.”
“Plenty of projects don’t read the answers.”

Leaking data out over DNS is old news. This crate goes further: it reads the replies, and when one carries the right marker, it does whatever the reply says.
chapters.close:
Beacon out, command back, executed in the same call — a working C2 channel hiding inside a metrics library.

One module left: a vendored C library that parses a “lightweight binary state” format. Everyone read the serializer. Nobody read the other half.

chapters.open:
“The serializer’s fine. I checked it line by line.”
“Nobody attacks the serializer.”

state_serializer.c is the textbook case: untrusted bytes read back into structures, and one “application specific” field type that the application never asked for.
chapters.close:
Four of four. Every sink, every trigger, every marker documented.

“One thing still bugs me,” the IR lead says. “Release builds were signed. So how did all of this end up in what we shipped?”

The answer lives in the build infrastructure: a self-hosted runner, tagged privileged.

chapters.open:
“Why is the runner privileged?”
“Docker-in-Docker builds. It was the easiest fix.”
“Easiest for who?”

The contributor knew exactly what that tag meant. Now the IR team has stood up an exec gateway onto the same runner — one command at a time inside the job sandbox, just like CI.

To show the board how bad this was, you’ll do what the attacker did: start inside the job, finish on the host.
chapters.close:
From inside a “sandboxed” job, you read a file only the host should see. The screenshot goes straight into the report.

“They’ll say that’s just the privileged runner,” someone warns. “The other one isn’t privileged.”

The other one has the Docker socket mounted inside it.

chapters.open:
“It’s unprivileged. No extra caps, no devices. It’s fine.”
“Then what’s /var/run/docker.sock doing in there?”
“…Builds need Docker.”

Whoever can talk to the daemon doesn’t need to escape their container. They ask for a new one, built however they like.

This is the last door. Walk through it.
chapters.close: The host gives up its last secret. There is nothing left of the attack you can’t explain.

finale.title: Case Closed
finale.text:
“So. Start to finish.”
“One trusted contributor. One commit. A beacon that only answers its own, a controller hidden behind dead-drops, a plan left in a diagram, four backdoors in three languages — and a build runner that handed over the host.”
“And Alex?”
“Alex trusted the wrong person. That’s not a crime. It’s just how open source works, until it isn’t.”

The report goes out that night. Coinnectar ships a clean release the next morning, the contributor’s access is gone, and the runner is no longer privileged.

The case file is closed. Your name is on it.
